title: Content-Safety System · Praxis AI
summary: Raised content-moderation accuracy from 49.6% to 80.8% on a 10,000-case internal benchmark, with a policy graph that gives decisions a traceable policy basis.
myRole: I own the content-safety system from requirements to launch. That covers the data and evaluation framework, the model context, fine-tuning and deployment of the classifier, decision thresholds, and the policy graph that connects each decision to the rule behind it.

caseStudy.problem: A moderation model has to catch violations without flooding reviewers with false alarms, and every allow, review or block decision has to point to the policy that justifies it. The starting point was 49.6% accuracy on the 10,000-case internal benchmark.

decisions.title: Improve accuracy on four fronts at once
decisions.detail: Accuracy rose through four coordinated changes: fine-tuning on human-verified golden data, a redesigned model context, a rebuilt data and evaluation framework, and tuned decision thresholds. The result reflects all four together, so none of them is credited on its own.

decisions.title: Keep policy separate from model scores
decisions.detail: A Neo4j policy graph links clauses, risk categories, scope and allow/review/block rules. It is kept separate from model scores and versioned by effective date, so decisions have a traceable policy basis.

decisions.title: Evaluate reproducibly, with a holdout
decisions.detail: A reproducible evaluation pipeline covers 10 domains and 14 scoring categories, with development/holdout separation, error analysis and safety checks.

decisions.title: Ship only verified models
decisions.detail: I fine-tuned Gemma 12B with PEFT/LoRA on GCP Vertex AI A100s and released it as versioned artifacts, with SHA-256 checks that block unverified models.

evidence.claim: Content-moderation accuracy rose from 49.6% to 80.8% on the 10,000-case internal benchmark.
On the same benchmark, missed violations fell by 73% and false positives by 96.9%.
Violation-detection F1 reached 0.865 on a 4,000-case holdout drawn from the benchmark.

tradeoffs: Thresholds trade missed violations against false positives. Reporting both rates alongside accuracy keeps that choice visible instead of hiding it in one number.
Keeping the policy graph separate from model scores means maintaining two versioned artifacts instead of one, in exchange for decisions whose policy basis is explicit and dated.
The holdout is drawn from the same benchmark, so it measures generalization within that benchmark's domains and categories. New policy domains need their own evaluation.

outcomes: Decisions have a traceable policy basis, kept separate from model scores and versioned by effective date.
SHA-256 checks on versioned model artifacts block unverified models.
A reproducible evaluation pipeline covers 10 domains and 14 scoring categories.
